sentence: Hives, or urticaria, is an itchy, raised rash that is usually triggered by a reaction to things such as food, pollen, insect bites or chemicals.
The rash can appear as raised bumps or patches in many shapes and sizes, and it can show up anywhere on the body.
It may itch, sting or burn.
Some people also have angio-oedema, which is swelling deeper under the skin.
note: BAD: angio-oedema often occurs in urticaria.

sentence: Swelling of the lips, eyelids or mouth is typical, and it is often painful rather than itchy.

sentence: Hives usually gets better within a few days.

sentence: In about half of the people with chronic spontaneous urticaria, the rash lasts for 6 to 12 months and then gradually disappears.
It can last considerably longer, and the course in any one person is unpredictable.
A rare cause is urticarial vasculitis, in which a very small percentage of people with an urticarial rash develop weals that last longer than 24 hours.
The BAD says that diagnosis is usually based on the history and the look of the rash rather than on tests.
Routine allergy tests are not necessary for most people with spontaneous urticaria who respond to antihistamines.
A UK guide based on NICE CKS says basic blood tests, such as a full blood count, may be used to rule out other conditions.
For physical types, the same guide says a provocation test such as the ice cube test may be used to confirm the diagnosis.
It also says that sun-related cases can be referred for ultraviolet light testing.
note: Allergy UK guide: referral to photodermatology for phototesting.

sentence: The same guide says the underlying cause should be identified and managed if possible.
The NHS says hives can often be treated at home and that a pharmacist can advise on antihistamines.
If the rash does not clear, a GP may prescribe menthol cream, antihistamines or steroid tablets, and may refer the person to a dermatologist.
For longer-lasting hives, the BAD says the aim of treatment is to control symptoms until the condition settles, rather than to cure it.

sentence: First-line treatment is a non-sedating antihistamine.
A person and their doctor may need to try different antihistamines to find the one that suits best.

sentence: Omalizumab is kept for severe cases and is available only in specialist clinics.
People who do not respond to antihistamines, or who are at risk of severe reactions, are referred for specialist review.
The BAD leaflet advises avoiding aspirin, ibuprofen and codeine unless they are essential, because they may make urticaria worse.
Where a trigger is known, avoiding or reducing it is part of care.
The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, if breathing is difficult, or if someone faints or cannot be woken.
It advises urgent advice from a GP or NHS 111 if the rash has not improved after 2 days, is spreading or keeps returning, or if there is a high temperature and the person feels unwell.
For children, NHS Healthier Together advises contacting a GP if symptoms last longer than six weeks or are hard to control with regular antihistamines.
Breathing problems with hives need urgent medical help.

sentence: What causes hives?
The NHS says hives is usually triggered by a reaction to things such as food, pollen, insect bites or chemicals.
Other triggers include infections, medicines, cold, heat, sweating, scratching and tight clothing.
Some cases have no identifiable cause, according to the BAD.
How long do hives last?
The NHS says hives usually gets better within a few days.
The BAD describes acute urticaria as lasting up to six weeks and chronic urticaria as lasting six weeks or more.
In about half of people with chronic spontaneous urticaria the rash clears within 6 to 12 months, but it can last longer.
When are hives an emergency?
The NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell, if breathing is difficult, or if someone faints or cannot be woken.
The BAD also says breathing problems need urgent medical help.
Are hives caused by an allergy?
They can be, but not always.
note: NHS: triggered by reaction to food, pollen etc.; BAD: some have no cause.

sentence: The NHS says hives can be a reaction to things such as food, pollen or insect bites.
The BAD says routine allergy tests are not necessary for most people with spontaneous urticaria who respond to antihistamines.
What is the difference between hives and angio-oedema?
Hives is a rash on the skin surface, while angio-oedema is swelling deeper under the skin.
